# Loading vectors fast

An embedding pipeline writes many floats, and the way they travel to Postgres decides whether a
load takes seconds or minutes. The lab loaded the same 50,000 rows of 384-dimension vectors in five
ways, from the ORM, which most code starts with, to binary `COPY`, which sends each vector in
pgvector's own binary format.

## Load methods

```
    method   | seconds | rows/s |  MB/s | vs orm
-------------+---------+--------+-------+--------
 orm         |    11.5 |   4347 |   6.7 | 1.0x
 executemany |     8.3 |   6024 |   9.3 | 1.4x
 copy_text   |     6.8 |   7358 |  11.3 | 1.7x
 copy_binary |    0.56 |  89363 | 137.3 | 20.6x
 pgpq        |    1.32 |  37746 |  58.0 | 8.7x
```

The rows of the table are, in order:

- `session.add_all(...)` through the ORM, which is what the app's ingest does and is fine for
  hundreds of rows
- Core `insert()` with a list of dicts, which uses the driver's `executemany`
- `COPY` in text format, which prints every float as text and parses it again on the server
- `COPY ... (FORMAT BINARY)` with pgvector's binary dumper, which sends floats as floats
- [pgpq](https://github.com/adriangb/pgpq), which converts Parquet through Arrow to the Postgres
  binary format and loads into a `FLOAT4[]` staging table, because pgpq has no `vector` type

Binary `COPY` was about twenty times faster than the ORM. pgpq also sends binary floats, but as a
Postgres array, which puts a 4-byte length in front of every element, so a `FLOAT4[]` takes twice the
bytes of a `vector` on the wire, before an `INSERT ... SELECT` even casts the rows.

Binary `COPY` needs one call to register the `vector` type with psycopg, and then it writes one row
at a time:

```python
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

register_vector(conn)  # teaches psycopg the vector type, binary dumper included
with conn.cursor() as cur, cur.copy("COPY items (title, embedding) FROM STDIN (FORMAT BINARY)") as copy:
    copy.set_types(["text", "vector"])
    for title, vec in rows:  # vec: a numpy float32 array
        copy.write_row((title, vec))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Index build order

An HNSW index is cheaper to build once over the loaded table than to maintain row by row during the
load, so it is best created after the data is in.
:::

## Reading vectors back

The lab also read the same table back as an `(n, 384)` numpy array in three ways:

```
 read back as numpy | seconds | rows/s |  MB/s | vs psycopg_rows
--------------------+---------+--------+-------+-----------------
 psycopg_rows       |    0.53 |  95004 | 145.9 | 1.0x
 copy_binary        |     0.4 | 125512 | 192.8 | 1.3x
 adbc_arrow         |    0.74 |  67889 | 104.3 | 0.7x
```

Binary `COPY ... TO STDOUT`, decoded in one numpy pass, was the fastest.
[ADBC](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/) has no `vector` type either, so the query casts the column to
`real[]`, which arrives as `list<float>` and pays the array overhead again. ADBC still fits when the
data is headed for Arrow anyway, as with Polars, DuckDB or Parquet.
